summary: Defines and registers +json-seq as a structured syntax suffix for media types built on JSON text sequences.

plainLanguage.summary: The +json-seq suffix tells an application that a media type is based on JSON text sequences. The application can use general JSON text sequence processing first, then apply any type-specific rules it needs.

questions: how to indicate json text sequences in media types
subtitle: A structured syntax suffix for media types based on JSON text sequences.

tldr.problem: A media type needs a way to signal that it is based on JSON text sequences so applications can use generic JSON text sequence processing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines and registers the +json-seq suffix for media types built on JSON text sequences.
tldr.outcome: An application can use generic JSON text sequence processing or add its own processing after that initial parsing. The RFC is Informational, not an Internet Standards Track specification.

today: RFC 8091 is an Informational document, not an Internet Standards Track specification. The unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Media Types Use Structured Syntax Suffixes
sections.content:
A media type can use a structured syntax suffix to show that it is based on an existing format. RFC 8091 defines +json-seq for media types based on JSON text sequences. JSON text sequences represent multiple JSON texts in one representation.

The RFC describes the suffix as serving the same use case as +json: it lets a media type signal its underlying syntax to applications that can process it generically.
sections.plainLanguage: A suffix at the end of a media type can identify the format that the type builds on. +json-seq identifies JSON text sequences as that format.

sections.title: How Applications Can Use +json-seq
sections.content:
A media type using +json-seq should use the suffix when parsing its JSON text sequence with generic processing produces a meaningful result. An application that encounters such a type can process the sequence generically if that is enough for its needs.

An application can also use generic JSON text sequence tools for initial parsing, then apply processing specific to the media type. The suffix identifies the underlying syntax; the RFC does not say that generic processing handles every type-specific meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: The suffix lets an application recognize when general JSON text sequence processing can help. The application can then add any processing specific to the media type.

sections.title: Registration and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC registers +json-seq, named “JSON Text Sequence,” in the Structured Syntax Suffix Registry maintained by IANA. Its registry entry refers to RFC 7464 for encoding considerations and security considerations.

RFC 8091 says the security considerations for JSON text sequences and JSON apply. The format provides no cryptographic integrity protection. Parsers must treat input as untrusted and fail gracefully; the RFC also discusses differences in parser behavior and how repeated parsing and re-encoding can affect signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA registers +json-seq for media types based on JSON text sequences. The format does not provide cryptographic integrity protection, so applications must handle untrusted input carefully.
